questions.q: What are the three key facts about Canada's system of government?
questions.a: It is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy
w: It is a republic, a dictatorship and a theocracy
It is a unitary state with a president
It is a one-party state with an elected king
questions.e: There are three key facts about Canada's system of government: our country is a federal state, a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy.

questions.q: What are the three levels of government in Canada?
questions.a: Federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal (local)
w: Senate, House of Commons and Supreme Court
questions.e: There are three levels of government in Canada: federal, provincial or territorial, and municipal (local).

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility of the federal government?
questions.e: The federal government is responsible for national defence, foreign policy, interprovincial trade and communications, currency, navigation, criminal law and citizenship.

questions.q: Which of these is a federal responsibility?
questions.e: Citizenship, currency, criminal law, national defence and foreign policy are federal responsibilities.

questions.q: Which of these is a responsibility of the provinces?
questions.e: The provinces are responsible for municipal government, education, health, natural resources, property and civil rights, and highways.

questions.q: Which of these is a provincial responsibility?
questions.e: Health, education, natural resources and highways are provincial responsibilities.

questions.q: Which two areas are shared by the federal and provincial governments?
questions.e: The federal government and the provinces share jurisdiction over agriculture and immigration.

questions.q: Federalism allows provinces to adopt policies suited to their own populations.
questions.e: Federalism allows different provinces to adopt policies tailored to their own populations and gives them flexibility to experiment with new ideas.

questions.q: Which law defined the powers of the federal and provincial governments in 1867?
questions.a: The British North America Act (Constitution Act, 1867)
questions.e: The British North America Act of 1867 defined the powers of the federal and provincial governments.

questions.q: What are the three parts of Parliament?
questions.a: The Sovereign (King or Queen), the Senate and the House of Commons
w: The Prime Minister, the Cabinet and the courts
The House of Commons, the Supreme Court and the police
The Governor General, the Premiers and the mayors
questions.e: Parliament has three parts: the Sovereign (Queen or King), the Senate and the House of Commons.

questions.q: How do members of the House of Commons get their seats?
questions.a: They are elected by the people
w: They are appointed by the Prime Minister
They are chosen by the King
questions.e: Members of the House of Commons, called Members of Parliament (MPs), are elected by the people, generally every four years.

questions.q: How are senators chosen?
questions.a: They are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister
w: They are elected by the people
They are chosen by the premiers
They are chosen by the Supreme Court
questions.e: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister.

questions.q: Until what age can senators serve?
questions.e: Senators are appointed and serve until age 75.

questions.q: What must happen for a bill to become law?
questions.a: It must be passed by both the House of Commons and the Senate and receive Royal Assent
w: It must be signed by the Prime Minister only
It must be approved by the Supreme Court
It must be approved by every province
questions.e: Bills must be passed by both houses of Parliament and receive Royal Assent, granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign, to become law.

questions.q: Who gives Royal Assent to bills passed by Parliament?
questions.a: The Governor General, on behalf of the Sovereign
questions.e: Royal Assent is granted by the Governor General on behalf of the Sovereign.

questions.q: In Parliament, how many readings must a bill pass in each chamber?
questions.e: A bill goes through first reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage and third reading in each chamber before Royal Assent.

questions.q: In Canada's parliamentary democracy, citizens elect representatives to make laws.
questions.e: In Canada's parliamentary democracy, the people elect members to the House of Commons and to the provincial and territorial legislatures. These representatives make laws, approve spending and can hold the government to account.

questions.q: Which of these do elected representatives in Parliament do?
questions.a: Pass laws, approve and monitor spending, and keep the government accountable
w: Run the courts and choose judges for every case
questions.e: Parliament passes laws, approves and monitors spending and keeps the government accountable.

questions.q: Who is the head of government in Canada?
questions.e: The Prime Minister is the head of government. The Sovereign is the head of state.

questions.q: Who is the head of state in Canada?
questions.e: Canada's head of state is a hereditary Sovereign who reigns in accordance with the Constitution. Today this is King Charles III.

questions.q: Who chooses the Cabinet ministers?
questions.e: The Prime Minister selects the Cabinet ministers and is responsible for the operations and policy of the government.

questions.q: What do Cabinet ministers do?
questions.a: They run federal government departments and prepare the budget and propose laws
w: They act as judges in the Supreme Court
They serve as officers in the armed forces
questions.e: Cabinet ministers are responsible for running federal government departments. The Cabinet prepares the budget and proposes most new laws.

questions.q: If the government loses a confidence vote in the House of Commons, it usually resigns.
questions.e: In responsible government, the Cabinet must keep the confidence of the elected House of Commons. If it loses a confidence vote, it must resign.

questions.q: What is the name of the largest party in the House of Commons that is not in government?
questions.a: The Official Opposition (His Majesty's Loyal Opposition)
questions.e: The opposition party with the most members in the House of Commons is the Official Opposition, or His Majesty's Loyal Opposition.

questions.q: Opposition parties work to oppose or improve government proposals.
questions.e: The role of opposition parties is to peacefully oppose or try to improve government proposals.

questions.q: Who represents the Sovereign in Canada at the federal level?
questions.e: The Sovereign is represented in Canada by the Governor General.

questions.q: Who appoints the Governor General?
questions.a: The Sovereign, on the advice of the Prime Minister
w: The voters in a national election
questions.e: The Governor General is appointed by the Sovereign on the advice of the Prime Minister, usually for five years.

questions.q: For how long is the Governor General usually appointed?
questions.e: The Governor General is usually appointed for five years.

questions.q: Who represents the Sovereign in each of the ten provinces?
questions.e: In each of the ten provinces, the Sovereign is represented by the Lieutenant Governor, appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister, usually for five years.

questions.q: Who represents the federal government in each of the three territories?
questions.e: The three territories each have a Commissioner who represents the federal government and plays a ceremonial role.

questions.q: The Sovereign is a symbol of Canadian sovereignty, a guardian of constitutional freedoms and a reflection of our history.
questions.e: The Sovereign is a symbol of Canadian sovereignty, a guardian of constitutional freedoms and a reflection of our history.

questions.q: The Prime Minister is Canada's head of state.
questions.e: The Sovereign is the head of state. The Prime Minister is the head of government.

questions.q: Canada's Sovereign is also the head of which association of countries?
questions.e: The Sovereign is head of the Commonwealth, an association of countries that are mostly former British territories.

questions.q: What is the head of a provincial government called?
questions.e: In each province, the Premier has a role similar to that of the Prime Minister in the federal government.

questions.q: What is the elected provincial legislature of Quebec called?
questions.e: In Quebec, the elected members of the provincial legislature are members of the National Assembly (MNAs).

questions.q: In Ontario, what are the elected members of the provincial legislature called?
w: Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs)
questions.e: Members of the provincial legislature are called MLAs in most provinces, MNAs in Quebec, MPPs in Ontario and MHAs in Newfoundland and Labrador.

questions.q: In most provinces, what are the elected members of the provincial legislature called?
questions.e: In most provinces, members of the provincial legislature are called Members of the Legislative Assembly (MLAs).

questions.q: In Newfoundland and Labrador, what are members of the provincial legislature called?
questions.a: Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs)
questions.e: In Newfoundland and Labrador, they are called Members of the House of Assembly (MHAs).

questions.q: Each province has its own elected legislature.
questions.e: In each province there is an elected legislature where provincial laws are passed.

questions.q: Who leads a municipal (local) government?
questions.e: A municipal government usually has a council that passes laws called 'by-laws'. It includes a mayor (or reeve) and councillors or aldermen.

questions.q: Which of these is usually a responsibility of municipal government?
questions.e: Municipalities are usually responsible for urban or regional planning, streets and roads, sanitation (such as garbage removal), snow removal, firefighting, ambulance and other emergency services, recreation facilities, public transit and some local health and social services.

questions.q: What are the laws passed by a municipal council called?
questions.e: Municipal councils pass laws called 'by-laws' that affect only the local community.

questions.q: Who governs First Nations reserves?
questions.e: Band chiefs and councillors have major responsibilities on First Nations reserves, similar to those of municipal governments.

questions.q: A person can run for Parliament as an independent, without belonging to a political party.
questions.e: Members of Parliament usually belong to a political party, but some run as independents and are not associated with any party.

questions.q: Senators are elected by the people every four years.
questions.e: Senators are appointed by the Governor General on the advice of the Prime Minister and serve until age 75.

questions.q: Education is a responsibility of the federal government.
questions.e: Education is a provincial responsibility.

questions.q: The Governor General is elected by Canadians.
questions.e: The Governor General is appointed by the Sovereign on the advice of the Prime Minister.

questions.q: The head of a provincial government is called the Prime Minister.
questions.e: The head of a provincial government is the Premier.
